Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

18 stepsFocal point: the sailboat and its white sails against the orange sky Light: the setting sun, low on the horizon just left of center; it lights the boat from the left and behindHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: Lay in the far hillFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Light the hull's top rimLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #2 round: Zigzag the mast's reflectionRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The sails; 2 The red hull. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 3.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 4.
  • Dry brush, first in step 6. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 7.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 9.
  • Liner work, first in step 12. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Pull-down, first in step 15.
  • Zigzag, first in step 17.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sky and sun 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 18 · The sky and sun, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is a little above the 3/4 mark on the side tape.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Sunset violet, Rose pink, then Sunset orange.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  7. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light is the setting sun, low on the horizon a little left of the middle, so the sky glows brightest around it. Keep the strokes long and level, and run the orange down past where the hill and sea will go.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 18 · The sky and sun, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little above the middle mark on the side tape, and its left side is a little left of the middle mark on the top tape.
  4. Paint: Pale sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Paint the disc in small circles with the tip of the brush, from its middle out to its round edge.
  7. It should leave a soft, round disc.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard or lumpy. Fix: go around the edge again with the same small circles and a lighter touch.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun sits a little left of the middle, about the width of a thumbnail. Keep it a clean circle; the sky's glow already surrounds it.

If it goes wrong.

The far hill and shore 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 18 · The far hill and shore, 1 of 2

Lay in the far hill

  1. Let the sky and sun dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is a little above the 3/4 mark on the side tape, and its left side is at the left edge.
  4. Paint: Dusky blue-violet.
  5. Mix enough Dusky blue-violet for this step and step 4; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Bend every stroke with the hill: along its slope from the rounded top down to the right, where it flattens into the shore.
  8. It should leave marks that follow the slope, which is what makes the hill look rounded.

Tip: The hill is highest about a quarter of the way in from the left, then slopes gently down to the right into a thin shore band that stops near the boat. Run the band's bottom a little below the shore line; the sea covers it. Keep it flat: it's far away.

Not checked yet

Motion. Bend every stroke with the shape: down each rib of a pumpkin from the top of the bump, around a balloon.

What it leaves. Marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

STEP 4 OF 18 · The far hill and shore, 2 of 2

Lay in the shore past the boat

  1. Let the far hill and shore, and the sky and sun dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is a little below the middle mark on the side tape, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Dusky blue-violet.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave flat, level bands that read as ground or water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.
  7. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: It's the same thin, level band as the hill's foot, only a finger's width tall. Keep its top edge straight and level.

The sea 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 18 · The sea, 1 of 2

Lay in the deep teal sea

  1. Let the far hill and shore, and the sky and sun dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is a little above the middle mark on the side tape.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave flat, level bands that read as ground or water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: Paint right up to the shore line and straight through where the boat and its reflection will go. Keep every stroke level so the water lies flat.

STEP 6 OF 18 · The sea, 2 of 2

Streak in the warm glints

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is at the middle mark on the side tape.
  3. Paint: Muted gold-olive.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Skim level streaks, more of them under the sun and fewer toward the edges; dry-brushed over teal they read as lighter, greener water. Let the teal show between them. Colors dry a little darker, so test this mix on the palette edge first.

The sun path 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 18 · The sun path, 1 of 2

Lay the first layer of the sun path

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is a little above the bottom edge, and its left side is a little right of the left edge.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Soft gray-teal, then Dull gold. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint, a light touch.
  5. Short, level dashes. Small and close together near the horizon, longer and wider apart lower down.
  6. It should leave short, flat, level marks with gaps of the water color between them.
  7. Watch out: The dashes smear into the water. The water underneath is still wet. Fix: paint them over dry water only.

Tip: Start right under the sun with short, close dashes, and let the path get wider as it comes down toward the bottom edge. This is where the painting can look messy; that's normal, it comes together in the next steps.

Brighten the middle of the path

  1. Let the sun path on the water and the sea dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

The sails 1 step

STEP 9 OF 18 · The sails, 1 of 1

Block in the two sails

  1. Let the sea, and the far hill and shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the 1/4 mark on the side tape, and its right side is a little right of the 3/4 mark on the top tape.
  4. Paint: Warm off-white.
  5. Mix enough Warm off-white for this step and step 16; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape: the tall left triangle. Then add the wider right triangle beside it, their inner edges meeting at the mast line.
  8. It should leave two triangles side by side, with a small gap or overlap where they meet.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The left sail is the taller, narrower triangle; the right one is wider at the bottom. Both meet along one straight vertical line where the mast will go, and their bottoms sit just above the hull.

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the picture shows smooth ribs; otherwise leave the segments visible.

Light the hull's top rim

The boat's reflection 4 steps

STEP 15 OF 18 · The boat's reflection, 1 of 4

Pull down the hull's reflection

  1. Let the hull and mast, and the sea dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is a little above the bottom edge, and its right side is a little right of the 3/4 mark on the top tape.
  3. Paint: Dark red-brown.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Load the brush, then wipe it until only a little paint is left.
  5. Stroke straight down, starting just below the thing being reflected.
  6. It should leave a soft, streaky, see-through reflection of the hull.
  7. Watch out: The reflection as sharp and detailed as the object. It looks like a mirror or a second picture. Fix: fewer details, softer edges, a thin dry brush.

Tip: Start right at the hull's bottom and pull the red-brown down through the whole reflection, narrowing it as you go, to a little below the 3/4 mark on the side tape. Keep it softer than the hull; the pale and the gray go over it next.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset, a low purple hill on the left, a pale sun just above the horizon with its orange path on the water, and a purple-to-orange sky.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: It is already a painted image filling the frame edge to edge, with no bars, text, border, or surroundings.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things besides the boat, which is the subject. No texture made of hundreds of items: the water's ripples and the sun path are rows of horizontal dashes, one repeated mark. No detail inside big shapes beyond that. About 7 parts (sky, sun, far hill and shore, water, sun path, boat, boat reflection), under max_parts 8.

Why: Every answer in step 0c is no, so the lesson is made from the photo.

A sunset seascape whose whole charm is three things: the purple-to-orange sky, the glowing sun path on teal water, and one small red boat with white sails and its broken reflection. The hard parts for a beginner are the wet sky blend, keeping the path narrow under the sun, and painting a reflection that's softer than the boat. The lesson should be about painting back to front and building water in layers.

Subject: A small red sailboat with white sails on teal water at sunset
Focal point: the sailboat and its white sails against the orange sky
Light: the setting sun, low on the horizon just left of center; it lights the boat from the left and behind

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. Far hill and shore
  3. Far shore right of the boat
  4. The sea
  5. The sails
  6. The red hull
  7. Mast and boom
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A beginner sunset seascape painted back to front on a white canvas: gradient sky, far hill, water with a sun path and a boat reflection. The paint-along technique has rules for exactly this (sky past the horizon, water reflections in order) and it is the only technique with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

No version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules), and the owner picked paint-along for beginner acrylic lessons.

How the paint recipes were worked out17 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order18 steps

Back to front, as the technique says: the sky first (run past the horizon), the sun on it, the far hill and shore, then the sea, the sun path on the dry sea, then the boat (sails, hull, mast) and last its reflection, because a reflection goes on after everything above the water is dry.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The farthest thing, blended wet in one go and run past the horizon so the land and sea go over it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    The sun sits on the sky, so it goes on once the sky is dry, before anything nearer.

  3. 3. Lay in the far hill

    The next thing back: the far hill and the shore band at its foot, flat and cool.

  4. 4. Lay in the shore past the boat

    The same shore band past the boat; its own outline, so its own short step.

  5. 5. Lay in the deep teal sea

    The sea is nearer than the land: a flat teal base before any light on it.

  6. 6. Streak in the warm glints

    Lighter warm streaks on the dry base give the water its surface.

  7. 7. Lay the first layer of the sun path

    The sun path sits on the dry sea: its dimmer first layer before the bright middle.

  8. 8. Brighten the middle of the path

    The second, brighter and narrower layer of the path, once the first is dry.

  9. 9. Block in the two sails

    The boat is the nearest thing; the sails go on before the hull and mast that sit in front of their bottom edge.

  10. 10. Block in the red hull

    The hull's base coat in front of the sails' foot.

  11. 11. Shade the hull's waterline

    The dark of the hull on its dry base coat, before the light.

  12. 12. Light the hull's top rim

    The lit rim on the side facing the sun, after the shading.

  13. 13. Line in the mast and boom

    The mast and boom go over the dry sails, as liner lines.

  14. 14. Catch the light on the mast

    The light on the mast after its dark line.

  15. 15. Pull down the hull's reflection

    The reflection goes on last, once the boat is dry: the hull's color pulled down first.

  16. 16. Pull down the sails' reflection

    The sails' paler reflection over the red, as the second reflection color.

  17. 17. Zigzag the mast's reflection

    The mast's wavy line on the dry reflection.

  18. 18. Cross the reflection with ripples

    Level ripple dashes last, breaking the reflection so it reads as water.

Filters it tried7 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams2 steps, free

Two block-in steps build a shaped object whole (the sails and the hull), so each gets a construction diagram. Everything else is a flat fill, a wet blend, a line, or one repeated mark the words and Where picture cover. While checking, five tips on the small boat and reflection passes named places the pictures don't paint; they were rewritten.

  • Step 9: Block in the two sails beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object appears whole in one step: two triangles meeting at the mast.

    Pieces: The taller left triangle first, then the wider right one beside it, both from the mast line.

  • Step 10: Block in the red hull beginner check

    Noticed: The boat's hull appears whole in one step, and where the bow starts isn't obvious.

    Pieces: A long flat rectangle along the waterline, then the curved bow piece on the right.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A wet gradient: the colors named top to bottom and the picture are enough.
  • Step 2: A small circle.
  • Step 3: One flat shape; its outline is the Where picture.
  • Step 4: A flat level band.
  • Step 5: A flat fill.
  • Step 6: One repeated level dry-brush mark.
  • Step 7: One repeated dash, placed by the Where picture.
  • Step 8: The same dash, narrower.
  • Step 11: Two short spots, placed by the tip and the Where picture.
  • Step 12: One short line.
  • Step 13: Two straight lines.
  • Step 14: A short line on the mast and boom.
  • Step 15: Straight-down pulls inside the outline.
  • Step 16: The same pull-down mark.
  • Step 17: One wavy line.
  • Step 18: One repeated level dash.
What the reviewer caught9 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Outline: the far shore band right of the boat would not join the hill's area after two rounds of points_in (the sails split it from the hill), so it went to the sky. Listing it as its own area part, far-shore, after the hill fixed it.
  • Every part found a library element (sky-blend, simple-shape, far-hills, water, sun-path, shaped-object, fine-lines, reflection), so no element was drafted. Three elements lost steps here because the finish had no extra color: water's ripple-dash step, and the sails' shade and light passes (paints --add sails found none).
  • Rewritten card lines: small-circles on the sun (its clouds wording); curved-strokes on the hill and the hull shade (pumpkin and balloon wording); build-from-pieces on the sails and hull; liner on the hull rim, mast, and mast light (its branches wording); pull-down and zigzag result lines (tree, post, plank wording). sky-blend's drafted paint order (violet, orange, pink) was wrong for this sky and was rewritten to violet, pink, orange.
  • My first tips for the small passes (hull shade, rim light, mast light, the reflection's red and pale) were written from the plan, not from the pictures, and the same-context review caught that each named the wrong place. Tips for passes should be written after reading the step picture.
  • The sea's glint pass also reveals a darker teal strip along the bottom edge that no paint covers; paints --add water found no distinct second color, so it's left as a known problem.
  • Steps 6 to 14 show the reflection's place as plain base-coat teal without glints until the reflection is painted (the parent's coat covers the child's place). A painter would streak the glints across it too; harmless, but the step pictures show a flat patch there.
  • No Agent tool in this run, so the text review was done in the same context (review_context: same).
